introduction: The Agriculture School-Based Assessment is a practical farm project. You plan and carry out a crop or livestock enterprise or an investigation, keep records as you go, and report on what you did, what it cost, what you produced and what you would change. Because the marks come from planning, doing, recording and evaluating, keep your diary up to date from the first week. Check the current CSEC syllabus and your teacher's guidance for the exact requirements for your session.

tasks.title: Choosing the enterprise
tasks.explanation: State the crop or animal you will produce, the plot or pen and its size, and justify your choice by referring to soil, climate, market and resources.

tasks.title: Calendar and inputs
tasks.explanation: Set out the operations in sequence with dates, and list the inputs, labour and equipment each will need.

tasks.title: Budget
tasks.explanation: Record quantities and prices of seed or stock, fertiliser or feed, chemicals, packaging and labour, and total the variable costs.

tasks.title: Field or pen diary
tasks.explanation: Keep dated entries for every operation, observation, problem and treatment. Include measurements - plant heights, weights, feed used, yields.

tasks.title: Results
tasks.explanation: Tabulate and graph your production data, compare performance with expectations, and explain the differences scientifically.

tasks.title: Conclusion
tasks.explanation: State the profit or loss, evaluate problems such as pests, weather or management errors, and recommend improvements for the next cycle.

sampleTitle: A plot of sweet pepper grown on a raised bed for one season

sample.body: Week 1: land preparation, compost applied at 4 kg per bed, seedlings raised in trays. Week 3: transplanting at 45 cm spacing with mulch. Weeks 4-12: weekly weeding, fortnightly foliar feed, scouting for aphids and thrips. Week 11: first harvest; successive harvests twice weekly until week 16.
sample.tips: Dates, quantities and the reason for each operation earn marks; vague plans do not.

sample.body: Total marketable yield was 96 kg from 40 plants, an average of 2.4 kg per plant. The unsprayed half of the plot yielded 38 kg and the scouted and sprayed half 58 kg, so pest control added about 50 per cent, at a chemical cost of $620. Fruit from the mulched section was larger and suffered less sun-scald, probably because soil moisture was steadier.
sample.tips: Compare a treatment with a control wherever possible, then explain the difference.

marking: Marks reward a justified choice of enterprise, a realistic activity plan and budget, complete dated records, accurate measurements and graphs, scientific explanation of results, and a candid evaluation with practical recommendations.
checklist: Inputs, labour and costs listed and totalled
Dated diary of operations and observations

completedSample.viewOnlyNote: For viewing and learning only. This is an original worked example written for CSEC Compass, not a real candidate's submission and not a CXC exemplar. The plot, the parish, the extension officer, the buyer and every price, weight and reading are invented to show what a full-mark Agriculture farm project report looks like. Read it, study how the records are kept, how the yields are worked out and how the losses are explained, then plan and run your own enterprise on your own plot. This sample cannot be copied.

categories.comment: Three enterprises are compared on soil, climate, market, resources and available knowledge, the site and soil are described from test-kit and jar readings taken before the bed was built, and the reason for the raised bed is tied to the clay subsoil found 20 cm down.

A dated calendar gives every operation, its inputs, its labour and the agronomic reason for the date, the bed specification is written to 21.6 square metres and 60 plants at a stated spacing and population, and the changes made to the plan during the season are recorded rather than hidden.

All 14 input lines are priced from the receipts and totalled at J$23,126.00, labour is recorded at J$2,000.00 a day for 5.00 person-days and totalled at J$10,000.00, and the two are added to give variable costs of J$33,126.00 for the season.

Dated diary entries from sowing to clearing give the operation, the measurement, the comparison and the action; plant height was measured on the same ten tagged plants, thrips counted weekly on 15 sticky traps, rain read from a gauge and irrigation counted in cans, and fruit was graded and weighed at the bed at every one of the seven pickings.

The 520 marketable fruits and 79.90 kg of picked fruit are tabulated picking by picking with mean fruit weights, yields are worked out a plant, a square metre and a hectare and compared honestly with the benchmark at the leaflet's own spacing, and the 12.50 kg of culls is broken into four causes each with a scientific explanation.

Profit of J$1,101.00 and a 3.2 per cent margin are worked out with labour costed at the casual rate, break-even is given both as 65.11 kg of fruit and as J$463.66 a kilogram, the return of J$220.20 a day is set against the J$2,000.00 a day labour rate, and seven specific improvements are recommended.

pages.heading: Cover page and contents
pages.body: This is the report on my CSEC Agriculture School-Based Assessment project: a block of sweet pepper (Capsicum annuum) grown on a raised bed at Sample Village, Clarendon (invented) for one season, from sowing on 10 April to the last picking on 20 October. The bed is 9.0 m long and 2.4 m wide, 21.6 square metres, and it carried 60 plants in 4 rows at 0.6 m by 0.6 m spacing. The site, the season, the extension officer, the buyer and every price, weight and reading in this report are invented for this worked example; the agronomy described is the agronomy a student would actually use. The report holds 25 sections and follows the order of the work: why this enterprise was chosen, what the site could give it, the plan and the budget, the dated record of everything done and seen, the production data tabulated and worked out, the science that explains the results, and an evaluation of the profit, the problems and what should change next season.

pages.heading: Selection: the enterprise chosen and how the choice was justified
pages.body: Three enterprises were possible for the one season I had. Each was judged on the same five points - the soil and the space available, the climate including the rainfall of the parish, the market within reach, the resources I had for seed, fertiliser and water, and the knowledge I could get from the extension officer. The comparison is set out below, and sweet pepper was chosen because it satisfied more of the five points than either alternative could. The bed could be built on ground that already drains well, so sweet pepper could be grown at the end of the dry season and picked in the dry weather when fruit rots less, the crop is widely eaten in Jamaica so a buyer was within walking distance, and the parish extension officer had sweet pepper results for comparable plots which gave me something to compare my own yield against. The choice was also a commercial one: the supermarket buyer agreed before planting to take graded fruit, so there was a market before there was a crop, which is the single mistake my father's neighbour made last year when he planted a crop and looked for a buyer afterwards.

pages.heading: Selection: the site, the soil and the water
pages.body: The plot is on rising ground about 40 m above the road, open to the east and shaded by a breadfruit tree on the west fence after 5 pm. A raised bed was chosen because the subsoil is a heavy clay that holds water after rain: raising the bed 30.0 cm lifts the root zone above it, and that was the single most important reason the bed was built before anything else. The site gives about ten hours of sun in the middle of the season. Soil was tested before the bed was built, with a simple test kit and a handful-of-soil test in a jar, and the readings are below. The pH was 5.8, which is too acid for sweet pepper - the crop takes up calcium and phosphorus best between pH 6.0 and 6.8 - so agricultural lime was worked in three weeks before transplanting and the pH was re-read at 6.4. The jar test showed roughly half sand, a third silt and the rest clay, which is a loam that holds water without waterlogging once it is raised and composted. Water is the other half of the picture: the standpipe is 30 m from the bed, the watering can holds 10 litres, and rather than guess how much the crop needed I recorded every watering through the season and set it against the rain gauge readings in section 14. Sweet pepper is shallow-rooted, so it needs water little and often rather than a soaking once a week, and the drip of a watering can into a mulched bed suits it well.

pages.heading: Plan of activities: the calendar with dates
pages.body: The calendar below was drawn up before the seed was bought and it is the plan the season was actually run to; where a date moved, the reason is written against it, because a plan that pretends nothing changed is worth less than one that records the changes. The sequence matters agronomically and each date was chosen for a reason, not by convenience. Lime went in three weeks before transplanting so that it had time to react with the soil. The nursery ran four weeks so that the seedlings went out at the six-to-eight leaf stage, which is when they transplant with the least check to growth. Mulch went down on the day of transplanting, while the plants were small enough to work around. The first sidedressing went on three weeks after transplanting, when the plants had made their first true flush of growth, and the calcium nitrate was split into three applications because calcium moves with water and a single dose would have been wasted in the first heavy rain. The last picking was set for the third week of October so that the bed could be cleared and replanted before the end of the year.

pages.heading: Plan of activities: the raised bed and how it was prepared
pages.body: The bed was built to a written specification rather than by eye, because the plant population and therefore the expected yield depend on the bed's dimensions. It is 9.0 m long by 2.4 m wide, raised 30.0 cm, with 4 rows 0.6 m apart and plants 0.6 m apart in the row, which gives 60 plants on 21.6 square metres. That is a population of 2.78 plants a square metre, or 27,800 plants a hectare. The extension officer's leaflet gives 25,000 to 30,000 plants a hectare for open-field pepper, so the planting was close to the top of that range, and I knew when I set it that close planting would later mean less airflow between the rows and more disease - which is exactly what happened, and it is written up in sections 17 and 18. The bed was built in layers: the top 15 cm of soil and subsoil was forked over and the stones taken out; 12.0 bags of well-rotted pen manure were spread and worked in to feed the crop and to open up the clay; the compound fertiliser was placed in a band 15 cm below the planting line rather than on the surface, so that the roots would grow down to it and not the weeds; the bed was shaped with sloping sides and the surface raked flat; and the plastic mulch was laid and buried at the edges the morning the seedlings went in. The plastic was chosen over straw after a small test: both suppressed weeds, but the straw kept the surface wet against the stems and the plastic warmed the bed and kept the fruit off the soil, which matters for a crop whose lower fruit can rot where it touches the ground.

pages.heading: Method: how the record was kept and the project run
pages.body: The record was kept in a bound book kept in the shed beside the bed, written up on the day and never from memory at the end of the week, and every entry follows the same four columns: what was done or seen, what it measured, what it was compared with, and what was done about it. The full diary is in sections 10 and 11. Weights were taken on a kitchen scale reading to 10 g, checked against a 1 kg bag of flour before the first picking; plant heights were measured with a metre rule from the soil surface to the growing point on the same ten tagged plants in every reading, which is the only way the readings mean anything; rainfall was read from a rain gauge emptied each morning at seven; and irrigation was counted in cans and written down as litres, which is why the water figures in section 14 can be set against the rain. Pests were monitored with 15 yellow sticky traps set among the rows and changed weekly, and the counts were used to decide when to spray rather than spraying on a calendar. Fruit was graded at every picking into marketable, meaning sound fruit at least 60 mm across and free of spots, and cull, meaning anything with rot, scald or damage, and the two weights were booked separately at the moment of picking. Grading at the bed rather than at the buyer is the reason the cull weight in this report is a real measurement and not an estimate, because the rejects never left the plot. At the end of the season the figures were worked out from those booked weights rather than from a total that might have been guessed at: J$67.40 kg of marketable fruit came from 520 fruits weighed at the bed, and J$12.50 kg was rejected and weighed the same way.

pages.heading: Materials and inputs: quantities and prices
pages.body: Every input was bought before it was needed and the receipt stapled into the record book, so the cost sheet is built from receipts rather than from memory. The one packet of seed cost more than the whole of the fertiliser, which is worth saying out loud: J$2,750.00 for a packet of hybrid seed against J$2,400.00 for 10 kg of compound fertiliser shows how much of the risk sits in the seed, and it is the reason the nursery was watered twice a day and watched so closely. The lime is on the list even though it is a soil treatment rather than a crop input, because without it the calcium and phosphorus in the fertiliser would have stayed locked up at a pH of 5.8. The plastic mulch is the largest single input line of all at J$2,850.00, a little more than the seed itself, and it is partly a cost that comes back: the mulch was lifted and stored at the end of the season and can be used for a second crop, which turns it from a cost of this crop into a cost shared between two. The water is charged at the standpipe rate for the 16.8 cubic metres actually applied, counted in cans, and the crates were bought rather than hired for the same reason as the mulch. The total of the input lines is J$23,126.00.

pages.heading: Materials and inputs: labour, and the variable cost total
pages.body: The labour record is kept in person-days at the rate the parish extension officer gave for casual farm labour, J$2,000.00 a day, and the whole 5.00 days were my own work with help from my father on the day the bed was built. Costing my own time at the casual rate is the honest thing to do even though no money changed hands, because a crop that only pays when the labour is free is not a crop that pays, and the difference between the two answers is the whole point of the evaluation in sections 20 and 21. The plan budgeted J$23,500.00 of inputs and J$15,000.00 of labour, 7.50 person-days at the same rate. The inputs came in at J$23,126.00, a little under the budget, and the labour at J$10,000.00, well under it, because the two operations that changed went in opposite directions: harvesting grew from the half day I had allowed for six pickings to a full day for seven, as the last three pickings had to be graded much more slowly once the cull proportion rose, while weeding fell from the day allowed to half a day because the plastic mulch did its job and the weekly monitoring took twenty minutes a visit rather than the half hour budgeted. Adding the inputs of J$23,126.00 to the labour of J$10,000.00 gives the total variable cost of J$33,126.00 for the season, which is the figure the revenue is set against in section 20.

pages.heading: Practical work: the nursery and transplanting record
pages.body: The nursery is where this crop was won or lost, because a seedling that is checked at transplanting is a plant that fruits a fortnight later than it should. 75 seeds were sown into a tray of potting mix on 10 April, one seed to a cell and no deeper than twice the seed's own diameter, and the tray was kept in the shade of the shed for the first four days so that the seedlings came up into soft light rather than full sun. 61 seeds came up, a germination of 81.3 per cent, which is normal for a hybrid blocky pepper and below the 90 per cent the packet promised; the ten that did not come up were all in the outside rows of the tray, where the mix dried fastest, which is the evidence for keeping the tray evenly watered rather than watering the middle. Thinning to one seedling a cell followed at the crown-leaf stage, and in the last week the tray was moved into full sun for increasing parts of the day, which is the hardening off that stops the seedlings scorching when they reach the bed. Of the 61 seedlings, 48 were strong enough to plant and 60 were actually planted at 0.6 m spacing on 12 May; the rest were kept in the tray as replacements and were not needed, because every planted seedling survived, an establishment of 125.0 per cent of the plants that went into the bed. Transplanting was done in the late afternoon into a bed that had been watered the evening before, with the seedling set so that its first true leaves sat just above the mulch.

pages.heading: Practical work: the field diary, part one
pages.body: The diary is reproduced below as it was written, with the measurements in the fourth column exactly as they were taken. Rain is given in millimetres and irrigation in litres, and the two together decide how the crop grew in that fortnight. The entries from transplanting to the end of June show the crop building its frame: the plants gained their height steadily, the first flowers opened in the first week of June and were dropped in the third week, which is normal for the first flush in hot weather, and the thrips counts on the sticky traps stayed low enough that no spray was needed until the middle of June. Reading these entries back at the end of the season, the two that matter most are 14 June, when the traps first jumped, and 21 June, when the neem spray was applied on the strength of the count rather than on a date in the calendar.

pages.heading: Practical work: the field diary, part two
pages.body: Part two of the diary covers the fruiting period and the end of the season, and it is the part that explains why the crop ended where it did. Three things changed in September. The rain arrived - 132.0 mm in that month against 44.0 mm in the driest month - and with it the bacterial spot; the fruit on the lower trusses began to touch the mulch and scald on the west side where the leaves had been lost; and the thrips count began to fall after the sprays and the cooler weather. Reading the entries together shows the sequence that the analysis in sections 17 and 18 works from: the sunscald followed the leaf loss, the leaf loss followed the bacterial spot, and both followed the wet spell at the end of a season in which the plants had already spent their vigour on a heavy crop. The last entry, 20 October, is the picking that paid least: 4.40 kg of marketable fruit at a mean of 112.82 g a fruit, against 5.30 kg rejected in the last two pickings together. Those two pickings gave 11.50 kg between them, 17.1 per cent of the season's marketable weight, and every small fruit in them had to be picked and graded one at a time, so they took far more work for each kilogram they gave than the pickings in August did.

pages.heading: Practical work: plant growth recorded week by week
pages.body: Plant height was measured on the same ten tagged plants at every reading, from the soil surface to the growing point, and the reading was taken before the first watering so that wet leaves did not change the figure. Height is only one measure of growth and on its own it says nothing about yield - a tall plant can be a plant that has run to leaves instead of fruit - so the readings are used in section 18 together with the harvest weights rather than on their own. The pattern in the table is the pattern of a healthy but finite crop. From transplanting to the eighth week the plants grew at 5.9 cm a week, which is the sort of steady rate the extension officer's figure describes for a well-grown blocky pepper, and by the eighth week the plants were 61.0 cm tall and the second flush of fruit was setting. After that the rate fell to 2.5 cm a week, so the plants added only 15.0 cm in the last six weeks, which is 31.9 per cent of all the extension they had made in the first eight weeks. That is not a fault in the crop; it is what a pepper plant does when it switches from growing leaves to filling fruit, and it is the reason the sidedressings in July were aimed at fruit size rather than at height.

pages.heading: Practical work results: pest and disease monitoring and treatments
pages.body: Pests were monitored rather than guessed at, and the two pest problems and the one disease are set out below with the count or incidence that was measured, the treatment applied and what happened after it. The trap counts in the first column are the mean number of insects caught a trap in the week; because the same 15 traps were set in the same positions and changed on the same day each week, the counts can be compared with one another and they show a clear rise, a clear peak and a clear fall. The rise began in the first week of June and reached its peak of 47 insects a trap at counting week twelve; after that the neem sprays, the removal of the worst-infested lower leaves and the cooler, wetter weather together brought the count down to 22 a trap by week sixteen, a fall of 53.2 per cent from the peak. The honest reading, however, is that the spraying trailed the pest: the first spray went on at a count of 19 and the peak still reached 47, which means the threshold I set - spray at 20 - was too high for a crop whose fruit was already set, and that recommendation is repeated in section 23. The disease tells a different story: bacterial spot could not be cured once the rain arrived, and what the copper did was slow it, which is why the cull weight went up in the last three pickings rather than the disease being stopped.

pages.heading: Practical work results: irrigation and rainfall against the crop's need
pages.body: The crop was watered by hand from a can, so the only way to know how much it received was to count, and the count is in the table. Over the season the crop had 529.0 mm of rain and 16.8 cubic metres of applied water, and the pattern matters more than the total. July was the driest month with only 44.0 mm of rain, so 4,200 litres were applied in that month and the water bill for the crop peaked with it; September was the wettest with 132.0 mm, so irrigation dropped to 1,900 litres and the problem changed from shortage to excess. Sweet pepper is shallow-rooted, so the aim was a steady supply rather than a soaking once a week, and the records show the crop was watered most days in the dry months and that the water went on in the evening so that less was lost to the sun. The failure to keep that steady supply in late June and the first week of July is the single most important line in this table: the soil was allowed to dry out between waterings for about ten days, and the blossom-end rot recorded on 12 July, 4.10 kg of it over the season, is the direct result. That is the clearest case in the whole project of a management error producing a measured loss, and it is why the first recommendation in section 23 is about water and not about pests or fertiliser.

pages.heading: Analysis results: the harvest record, picking by picking
pages.body: Seven pickings were taken between 30 July and 20 October and each was weighed at the bed before it left the plot. The season produced 520 marketable fruits weighing 67.40 kg, and a further 12.50 kg was rejected, so 15.6 per cent of everything picked was thrown away or sold off cheaply. The shape of the pickings is the first thing to read. Fruit weight rose from 7.40 kg at the first picking to a peak of 14.00 kg on 27 August, and then fell away to 4.40 kg at the last picking, which is the ordinary curve of a blocky pepper carrying three flushes of fruit. The second thing to read is the mean fruit weight, and it tells a different story from the totals. Mean fruit weight fell almost without a break: it was 145.1 g at the first picking on 30 July, right at the top of the large grade the buyer wanted, and 112.8 g at the last picking on 20 October, a fall of 32.3 g a fruit across the season. So the season's mean of 129.6 g hides a trend: the early fruit filled well and the late fruit did not, because those plants were filling fruit on a shrinking leaf area, and the small fruit still had to be picked, graded and delivered one at a time. The third thing to read is the cull column, and this is where the season turned: the first three pickings produced 2.90 kg of rejects and the last two produced 5.30 kg, an increase of 82.8 per cent, with 42.4 per cent of the whole season's rejects coming from those last two pickings. The reason is in section 17 and the science is in section 18.

pages.heading: Analysis results: yield per plant, per square metre and per hectare
pages.body: One total weight on its own says nothing about how well the bed performed, so the yield was worked out in the three ways that can be compared with something. There were 60 plants on 21.6 square metres, and the marketable harvest of 67.40 kg gives 1.12 kg a plant, 3.12 kg a square metre and 31.2 tonnes a hectare. The per-plant figure is the one to judge the crop itself by, and it is good: the extension officer's range for a well-managed open-field crop is 1.0 to 1.5 kg a plant, and this crop came in at 1.12 kg, inside that range and close to its middle. The per-hectare figure, 31.2 tonnes, has to be read with the spacing in mind. The leaflet's range is 25.0 to 35.0 tonnes a hectare, so this crop looks as though it beat the top of the range - but it was planted at 27,800 plants a hectare against the 25,000 the leaflet's figure assumes, and a hectare carrying a fifth more plants should be expected to yield a fifth more. Worked out on a per-plant basis, which takes the crowding out of the comparison, the crop is inside the range rather than above it, and the extra plants bought nothing except more disease. That is the honest way to compare the two, and it is the reason the plan's planting density is on the list of things to change in section 23. Setting the 14 input lines of J$23,126.00 against the marketable harvest gives a cost of J$343.12 of bought inputs for every kilogram of fruit grown, and J$491.48 a kilogram once the labour is counted, which is the figure that decides whether this crop was worth growing at all.

pages.heading: Analysis results: why 12.50 kg of fruit was rejected
pages.body: Rejecting 12.50 kg out of 79.90 kg picked is the biggest single failure of the season, and it is worth more to write it up honestly than to report a clean crop that did not exist. Every rejected fruit was looked at and put into one of four groups as it was picked, and the groups are in the table with the science that explains each one. Two of the four were management errors on my part and two were not. Blossom-end rot, 4.10 kg, was mine: it is not a disease but a calcium shortage inside the fruit, and calcium reaches the fruit only in the water the plant takes up, so when the bed was allowed to dry out between waterings in late June the fruit at the flower end was starved of it while the leaves went on taking their share. Sunscald, 3.20 kg, followed from the bacterial spot that stripped the leaves off the west side: a fruit with no leaf over it is cooked by the afternoon sun, and that is why the scald appeared on the same side of the bed as the worst spot. Bacterial spot itself, 2.90 kg, was partly mine and partly the weather: the organism was almost certainly carried on the leaves from the wet spell in September, but I had planted at 2.78 plants a square metre, and closer rows keep the leaves wet for longer after rain, which is exactly what this disease needs. The undersized fruit, 2.30 kg, was the subsoil: the western end of the bed is shallower over the clay, those plants had less root room and less water, and they filled fruit that never reached the grade. Set against the whole harvest, the culls cost J$6,000.00 at the marketable price, which is more than the whole profit the crop made.

pages.heading: Discussion: explaining the growth curve and the yield curve
pages.body: The growth readings in section 12 and the harvest weights in section 15 are two views of the same plant behaviour, and putting them together explains the whole season. From transplanting the plants grew at 5.9 cm a week and built a frame of leaves and roots; the first flowers that opened in the first week of June were dropped, which is what pepper does in heat, and that cost about ten days because fruit set only began properly on the second flush. Once fruit set began, growth slowed to 2.5 cm a week - the plants had stopped building and started filling - and the harvest weights followed the same logic with a lag of about two weeks. Picking climbed to its peak on 27 August and then fell, because a pepper plant carries a finite number of fruits and a finite root system, and after three flushes it has spent its vigour. That is the scientific reason the last two pickings produced small fruit: the plants were filling fruits from a smaller leaf area because the spot had stripped leaves, and the fruit that did fill was competing with fewer resources, so mean fruit weight fell from 145.1 g to 112.8 g. There is one more relationship worth naming, because it ties the whole report together: water, calcium and blossom-end rot. Calcium is taken up passively, carried in the transpiration stream, and it cannot move from an old leaf to a young fruit the way nitrogen can; the fruit at the end of a truss and the fruit on the plant under the most stress get the least of it. That is why 4.10 kg of fruit was lost to a shortage that had nothing to do with how much calcium nitrate was applied and everything to do with whether the soil was kept evenly moist. In the same way, the bacterial spot explains the loss of 3.20 kg to sunscald: the cause was a leaf disease two steps removed from the damage, and treating it as a sunscald problem would have been treating the symptom.

pages.heading: Discussion: how the crop performed against the plan and the benchmark
pages.body: Before planting I set out what I expected, and this section sets the plan against what actually happened, because the differences are more instructive than the totals. The plan was for 75.00 kg of marketable fruit, which was 1.25 kg a plant over 60 plants. The bed produced 67.40 kg, or 89.9 per cent of the target, at 1.12 kg a plant. Of the eight measures in the table below, six came in below the plan and two above it. Fruit size came in one grade low - 129.6 g against the 140.0 g planned - but the buyer took it as large grade without a deduction, so that miss cost nothing directly. The cull proportion was the serious miss: 15.6 per cent against 8.0 per cent, nearly twice the loss allowed for, which is what turned a comfortable profit into the thin one worked out in section 20. Revenue reached 95.1 per cent of the figure in the plan, and the surplus came in at J$1,101.00 against the J$5,000.00 planned. Reading the misses together, they are one miss: the season was lost to water and to leaves. The fortnight of uneven watering in late June started the blossom-end rot, the wet spell in September carried the spot, and the spot cost the leaves that would have shaded the fruit and filled it. None of the three was a failure of the plan's structure - the calendar, the spacing calculations and the budget were all sound and all followed - and that is worth saying plainly, because a student reading this should understand that a well-planned crop can still be beaten by a fortnight of water and a fortnight of rain.

pages.heading: Evaluation: the cost sheet, the revenue and the profit
pages.body: The enterprise made a profit of J$1,101.00 on revenue of J$34,227.00 and variable costs of J$33,126.00, which is a margin of 3.2 per cent. The marketable fruit was sold to one buyer at J$480.00 a kilogram and the 12.50 kg of rejects to a sauce maker at J$150.00 a kilogram, which is worth noting: the rejects were not a total loss. Without the J$1,875.00 they brought in, the season would have ended J$774.00 in the red, so grading them out separately and selling them was worth the trouble. A hotel offered J$560.00 a kilogram, which would have added J$5,392.00 to the revenue, but it wanted two deliveries a week and I could not make them, so the firm price from the supermarket was taken. The figure this section turns on, though, is the return on my own labour: J$1,101.00 for 5.00 person-days of work is J$220.20 a day, against the J$2,000.00 a day casual labour is paid in the parish, a shortfall of J$1,779.80 a day. In other words the crop paid better than nothing but it did not pay the labour that produced it, and that is the honest headline for the season. If no value is put on my own time the cash position was a surplus of J$11,101.00, which is real money, but a business cannot run on unpaid family labour indefinitely; the answer is not a higher price, because J$480.00 a kilogram is a fair farm-gate price, it is more kilos from the same labour, which is what a second bed and a lower planting density are for.

pages.heading: Evaluation: the break-even analysis
pages.body: Break-even turns the profit into a target a farmer can aim at, and it was worked out two ways. Counting the cull sales as income, the bed had to produce 65.11 kg of marketable fruit to cover its variable costs. It produced 67.40 kg, so it cleared break-even by 2.29 kg, which is a margin of 3.4 per cent. Put the other way round, J$463.66 a kilogram was the price needed to cover the costs at the yield actually achieved, against the J$480.00 a kilogram received, so the crop cleared the price it had to clear by J$-16.34 a kilogram - a margin so thin that it explains the whole result. Two conclusions follow, and both are in the recommendations. First, the margin is so narrow that a single extra cull weighing a few kilograms would have turned the profit into a loss: at J$480.00 a kilogram, losing 2.29 kg more fruit would have wiped out the season's profit completely. Second, break-even was passed by volume rather than by price, which means the way to make the enterprise worthwhile is to spread the fixed elements of the cost - the seed packet, the crates, the mulch and the deliveries - over two beds rather than one. The seed packet alone costs J$2,750.00 and it holds far more seed than 60 plants, and the mulch and crates are both reusable, so a second bed of the same size would add input cost but almost no fixed cost, and the profit would rise by much more than half.

pages.heading: Evaluation: the problems met and how each was managed
pages.body: Five problems affected the crop and each is set out below with its cause, what was done at the time, what it cost and what should have been done instead. The first and the largest was my own: the bed dried out between waterings for about ten days in late June and the first week of July, and the blossom-end rot that followed cost 4.10 kg of marketable fruit. The cause was not really the weather, it was the way the watering was organised - I watered when the surface looked dry rather than on a fixed amount, so on the days I was busy the plants went without. The second was the bacterial spot, which was a mixture of weather and my own close spacing, and which cost 2.90 kg directly and a further 3.20 kg of fruit through the leaf loss that led to sunscald. The third was the thrips, where the honest failure was the threshold rather than the spraying: I set the spray level at 20 insects a trap and the count doubled before the first spray went on. The fourth was fruit size: the crop mean of 129.6 g against a 140.0 g target came from carrying too many fruits on too few leaves after the spot, and I did not thin the early fruit. The fifth was the labour estimate: harvesting took a full day for seven pickings instead of the half day allowed, because grading slowed down as the cull proportion rose, and that single change used most of the slack in the plan's other labour lines.

pages.heading: Limitations and improvements
pages.body: The limitations below are written as they are, because a report that claims a perfect season teaches nobody anything, and because each of them leads to a change that would make the second crop better than the first.
bullets: Watering was judged by eye instead of by measurement, and the bed dried out for about ten days in late June; that error alone accounts for 4.10 kg of the loss. Improvement: a written watering schedule of a set number of cans a day, ticked off in the diary, and a cheap drip line if one can be bought.

The planting density of 27,800 plants a hectare was at the top of the extension officer's range and left too little airflow between the rows for the wet September. Improvement: plant the same bed at 25,000 plants a hectare, which reduces the population to about 54 plants on this bed and gives the rows room to dry.

The spray threshold of 20 thrips a trap was set from a textbook figure rather than from the crop's own stage, and the count doubled before the first spray. Improvement: once fruit is set, treat at 10 insects a trap and keep a written threshold at the top of the diary page.

The calcium nitrate was applied in three doses but nothing checked whether the soil was still holding calcium, because there was no soil test after the initial one. Improvement: a second kit test at first fruit set, and a little gypsum in the bed at preparation if the pH is above 6.5.

The bed was planted as one block with no control, so no treatment could be compared with an untreated strip. Improvement: split the bed and run a comparison, for example mulch against no mulch or two spacings, which would turn a report into a real investigation.

The mulch, the crates and the seed packet were all bought for one bed. The seed packet holds far more seed than 60 plants and the mulch and crates are reusable, so their cost was carried by one crop when it should be shared. Improvement: plant a second bed of the same size next season, which almost doubles the yield while barely raising the input cost, and write the shared cost into the budget that way from the start.

Weights were taken on a kitchen scale reading to 10 g, which is fine for crates of fruit but too coarse for single fruits. Improvement: borrow the school's 1 g balance for one picking and record individual fruit weights, which would let the grade distribution be graphed properly.

pages.heading: Conclusion
pages.body: The bed of 60 sweet pepper plants on 21.6 square metres at Sample Village, Clarendon (invented) produced 67.40 kg of marketable fruit and 12.50 kg of rejects between 30 July and 20 October, which is 1.12 kg a plant and 31.2 tonnes a hectare on paper. The crop made a profit of J$1,101.00 on revenue of J$34,227.00, a margin of 3.2 per cent, and it cleared break-even by 2.29 kg, or 3.4 per cent. Measured as a return on the work, though, the season was not a success: J$1,101.00 for 5.00 person-days is J$220.20 a day against the J$2,000.00 a day casual labour is paid, so the season's whole profit is what 0.55 of a day's hired work would have paid. The cause of that is not the market and not the plan; it is 12.50 kg of rejected fruit, 15.6 per cent of everything picked, and 81.6 per cent of that loss traces back to two things I controlled - watering that was judged by eye instead of measured, and a planting density that left the rows too close for a wet September. If I grew the bed again I would water to a written schedule, plant at 25,000 plants a hectare, treat thrips at 10 insects a trap once fruit is set, and plant a second bed so that the seed, the mulch and the crates are paid for by twice the fruit. On the plan's own terms the season came in at 89.9 per cent of the target yield, and I would expect a second cycle to clear the target without any change except those four.

examinerNotes: This subject is marked out of 42 under six tasks, and the report answers each one with real work: a justified enterprise choice, a dated calendar, a costed budget, a dated record with measurements, production data worked out and explained scientifically, and an evaluation that names a loss and says why.

The strongest feature is that the report measures rather than estimates. The bed's 21.6 square metres and the spacing give 60 plants; the pickings give 67.40 kg marketable and 12.50 kg of culls; the rain gauge and the can count give 529.0 mm and 16.8 cubic metres of water; and every yield figure, the cost a kilogram, the break-even yield and the break-even price all come from those same weighed and counted numbers, so the tables and the prose agree.

The analysis goes beyond arithmetic into cause and effect: blossom-end rot is explained as a calcium transport problem caused by uneven watering rather than as a disease, and the sunscald is traced two steps back to the bacterial spot that removed the shading leaves. A marker can see the candidate understands the crop, not just the calculations.

The evaluation is candid about money as well as about the crop. It states that the profit of J$1,101.00 is a return of J$220.20 for each of 5.00 days of work against a casual rate of J$2,000.00, that break-even was cleared by only 2.29 kg, and that 2 kg of extra rejects would have wiped out the profit. Plot, parish, prices and all readings are invented placeholders; run your own enterprise on your own plot with your own records.
